source: Hugging Face daily papers, 2026-08-01 to 2026-10-01, arXiv primary category cs.CL, with a code link; upvotes as of 2026-10-02
checked: the 51 most upvoted, by reading the paper and repository (code was not run)

papers.title: StudentSim: Training LLM-based Student Simulators
papers.what_it_is: StudentSim trains per-student simulators by LoRA fine-tuning Qwen3-4B-Instruct in two stages (pooled across students, then per-student) on chess, L2 English writing and middle-school math records. Experiments measure behavioral fidelity and guidance responsiveness against prompted GPT-5.4/GPT-4o and Maia2, plus a chess tutor trained by RL against the simulator with human expert ratings.
papers.code_notes: github.com/microsoft/StudentSim holds a real Python package (studentsim/ with training, eval, baselines, tutor_rl, data builders, CLI entry points and YAML configs). However no data or checkpoints are usable today: data/chess/README.md says the Hugging Face upload "has not landed yet" and still has a <HF_ORG>/<HF_DATASET> placeholder; the L2 (EFCAMDAT) and math (FoundationalASSIST) data require provider agreements; a Hugging Face search for StudentSim returned no datasets or models, so no Stage-1 adapters are released.
papers.feasibility_notes: The core method is open (Qwen3-4B LoRA), but the only redistributable data (chess) is not yet published, the other two domains are licence-gated, and no Stage-1 adapter is released; Stage 1 is configured for 8 GPUs on 100k records, so retraining it within 45 minutes on one A100 is doubtful. Azure OpenAI is needed only for baselines, guidance-text generation and the math data build, not for the simulator itself. If the chess data lands, a Stage-2 ablation (about 12 gradient steps per student) would become feasible.
papers.followup_evidence: None found. Semantic Scholar API returned citationCount 0 with an empty citations list. Web searches for "StudentSim" with builds on/extends/follow-up returned only the paper, news coverage and earlier related work (2601.05473, 2601.04025, 2608.17150 all predate it).

papers.title: Compile by Training: Turning Natural-Language Specifications into Local Neural Functions
papers.what_it_is: Compile by Training turns a natural-language function specification into a local neural function by having teacher LLMs synthesize input-output examples and then training a rank-64 LoRA adapter (100 steps, about a minute) on a frozen Qwen3-0.6B interpreter, initialized from the earlier Program-as-Weights fast compiler. The main experiment is on FuzzyBench-Hard, reaching 83.6% semantic accuracy as judged by a GPT-5.5 judge; it is an EMNLP 2026 system demonstration.
papers.code_notes: github.com/programasweights/compile-by-training is small but real: one 1,270-line compile.py (teacher synthesis, LoRA training, GGUF packaging), README, MIT licence, CI workflow. It contains no evaluation or benchmark code, so FuzzyBench-Hard scoring and the judge would have to be rebuilt. FuzzyBench data is on Hugging Face (yuntian-deng/fuzzy_bench_verified, wtzhang-nlp/fuzzy_bench); the interpreter and compiler weights are under the programasweights organisation there.
papers.feasibility_notes: As published the method needs paid APIs: teachers are GPT-5.4-mini and GPT-5.5 via OPENAI_API_KEY, and the metric uses a GPT-5.5 judge. Follow-ups fit only by deviating: compile.py reads TEACHER_API_URL, so a local open teacher of at most 8B served through an OpenAI-compatible endpoint can replace the teachers, and training takes 50-100 s per spec with about 40 GB memory. Example: on 10 FuzzyBench specs, compare mapper-only versus compile-by-training with an open teacher across example counts or steps, scored by exact match. Caveat: step 1 calls the hosted programasweights.com compile endpoint (free, rate-limited); I did not verify that a local replacement works.
papers.followup_evidence: None found. Semantic Scholar API returned citationCount 0 with an empty citations list. Web search for "Compile by Training" with Program-as-Weights/follow-up returned only the paper, its Hugging Face page and one blog summary. The paper is itself a follow-up to Program-as-Weights by the same group.

papers.title: NCP-ArchPreview Technical Report: Moving towards Latent Space Language Models through Next Concept Prediction
papers.what_it_is: NCP-ArchPreview is a technical report on an 8.9B-parameter latent-space language model trained jointly with next-token prediction and Next Concept Prediction over a product-quantized concept vocabulary, pretrained on 5.73T Dolma-3 tokens. Experiments compare it with OLMo-3-7B on pretraining loss and downstream benchmarks (GSM8K, SciQ, Core88, RULER, HELMET), plus VQ-module domain adaptation and a speculative-decoding drafter.
papers.code_notes: github.com/LUMIA-Group/ncp_olmo_eval is a real, runnable evaluation toolkit (src/, tests/, docker/, configs/, scripts/, PyPI release 0.1.1) built on vLLM, but it is evaluation only. It has no training or model-architecture code for the method; inference code lives in a separate vLLM fork. Checkpoints are public on Hugging Face (ArchSpace-Collection), all 8.9B.
papers.feasibility_notes: The only released NCP models are 8.9B parameters, above the 8B cap, and the contribution is large-scale pretraining that cannot be touched in 45 GPU-minutes. The repo's evaluation plans are specified as 1x8 GPU jobs with a pinned vLLM fork and sealed images, and no training code is released, so follow-ups would be limited to partial re-evaluation of an over-limit model.
papers.followup_evidence: No follow-up paper found, but unverified through Semantic Scholar: the API returned HTTP 429 on every attempt for this id. Web searches for "NCP-ArchPreview" with Next Concept Prediction/replication/extends found only the report, news coverage, the earlier NCP paper it builds on (arXiv 2602.08984), and a third-party GitHub replication with no paper (tachytelicdetonation/NCP-64M, 0 stars, created 2026-09-13).

papers.title: NeoHorse-1: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement via Agentic Post-Training with Routing Harness
papers.what_it_is: Introduces NeoHorse-1, a family of 4B and 9B open-weight agent models post-trained on 10^5-10^6 trajectories logged from a routing harness over a heterogeneous model pool, using a three-stage curriculum and routing-guided on-policy distillation. The main experiment is benchmark evaluation of the post-trained models against their base models on about eleven agentic, tool-use, coding and instruction-following benchmarks.
papers.code_notes: https://github.com/TokenRhythm/NeoHorse exists and is not empty, but it is a model-release repo: README, technical report PDF, two short inference examples (examples/chat.py, examples/tool_call.py) and a jev/ directory with inference/deployment adapters (vLLM, SGLang, native runtime) for the NeoHorse-Jev-4B decision model. I listed the full file tree through the GitHub API: there is no training code, no routing harness, no trajectory-to-training-data pipeline, no data, and no benchmark evaluation harness. So nothing that implements the paper's method or reproduces its experiments.
papers.feasibility_notes: The method itself (large-scale post-training on proprietary harness trajectories from an undisclosed model pool) cannot be touched in 45 GPU-minutes and neither the data nor the pipeline is released; the 9B model also exceeds the 8B cap. The only thing that fits is inference-only evaluation of the released 4B weights against the base model on a small public benchmark (e.g. IFEval or HumanEval), which tests the checkpoint rather than the paper's idea, so I judge it not informative enough.
papers.followup_evidence: None found. Semantic Scholar API returned citationCount 0 and an empty citations list. Web search for "NeoHorse-1" agentic post-training routing harness with follow-up/builds-on terms returned only the paper itself, aggregator pages and blog explainers (emergentmind, mindstudio, alphaxiv, pith), no later paper.

papers.title: Omni-IO Skills: Harnessing Your Agent Omni-Native
papers.what_it_is: Presents Omni-IO Skills, a plug-and-play harness of 27 hierarchical skills plus an MCP tool server, dependency-graph orchestration and an asset registry that lets an existing agent understand and generate images, video, audio, documents, 3D, code and web content. The main experiment loads the harness into GPT-5.6 Sol and Claude Sonnet 5 as host agents and measures input-support rate and quality scores on the 90-instance UniM-90 multimodal benchmark.
papers.code_notes: https://github.com/any2any-mllm/Omni-IO-Skill contains real code as far as I could tell from the repo page: skills/, expert/, scenarios/, orchestration/, an MCP server (mcp/server.py), config/ for provider bindings and credentials, requirements.txt, install instructions for Codex and Claude Code, and 20 worked examples. I only inspected the top-level listing and README, not individual files, and did not see a script that reproduces the UniM-90 evaluation.
papers.feasibility_notes: The host agents in every experiment are hosted frontier models (GPT-5.6 Sol, Claude Sonnet 5), and the skills call external image/video/audio generation and transcription providers through API keys; the paper describes no local or open-model setting. It is a multimodal agent-tooling paper rather than a language-model one, and its evaluation cannot be reproduced without paid APIs.
papers.followup_evidence: None found, but only partly verified. The Semantic Scholar API returned HTTP 429 on every attempt (five tries with backoff), so I have no citation list. Web search for "Omni-IO Skills" omni-native agent UniM-90 with extends/builds-on terms returned only the paper, the repo, the Hugging Face paper page and news/aggregator pages. The paper was posted 2026-09-25, one week before this check.

papers.title: Post-Training Leaves Behavioral Shadows on Unrelated Decisions
papers.what_it_is: Shows that a student model can pick up a teacher's post-trained capability from task-unrelated data: Active Taskless Distillation selects prompts where the shared public ancestor is nearly indifferent between two ordinary words and trains the student on the teacher's single-word choice. The main experiment trains rank-16 LoRA students of Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct on 5,664 such single-word answers from a code-tuned teacher and compares HumanEval+ pass@1 with a nuisance-matched control (51.22% vs 45.88%, +5.34 pp, 95% CI [1.22, 9.60]), with further tests on GSM8K, multiple-choice QA sets and other small models (Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-4B, Llama-3.2-1B).
papers.code_notes: https://github.com/myboker/ATD is real, runnable code for the main experiment (file tree and README read directly): run.py entry point with reproduce/verify/train/evaluate/analyze stages, atd/ package (train.py, evaluate.py, controls.py, analyze.py, data.py), unit tests, requirements, the two released training arms (data/signal.jsonl and data/exact.jsonl, 5,664 rows each), carrier metadata, and frozen EvalPlus outputs for four seeds. Limits stated in the README: it covers only the main Qwen2.5-1.5B HumanEval+ experiment; the private teacher, the carrier-prompt collection step, and the configs/data for the other controls, other benchmarks and other models are not released. I did not execute anything.
papers.feasibility_notes: Each student is a rank-16 LoRA on a 1.5B model trained for 157 steps at effective batch 128 on single-token targets, followed by greedy generation on 164 HumanEval+ tasks, so one signal/control pair should fit comfortably in 45 A100-minutes; the full four-seed run of eight students might not, and the paper gives no timing so this is my estimate. Example follow-up: train one signal and one exact-control student from the released arms and evaluate both on a benchmark not in the release (e.g. MBPP+ or a GSM8K subset), or vary the number of training rows or LoRA rank to see how the gap scales. Experiments needing a new teacher or new carrier prompts would require rebuilding the unreleased collection step.
papers.followup_evidence: None found, but only partly verified. The Semantic Scholar API returned HTTP 429 on every attempt (five tries with backoff), so I have no citation list. Web searches for "Active Taskless Distillation" ATD "behavioral shadows", and for "Behavioral Shadows" with "taskless distillation"/"subliminal learning" and extends/replicates terms, returned only the paper, its repo, aggregator pages and a news explainer; the subliminal-learning papers that surfaced (arXiv 2604.25783, 2606.00995, 2608.05734) all predate it and are prior work. The paper was posted 2026-09-24, eight days before this check.

papers.title: OpenART: Scaling Agent Red Teaming via Open-Ended Environment Evolution
papers.what_it_is: OpenART is an executable benchmark/arena for red-teaming tool-using coding agents: 10K+ stateful scenarios (median ~97 tool calls) plus EMHA, a black-box attacker that evolves the environment state while task and safety contract stay fixed. The main experiment measures attack success rate across 75 agent-runtime x model configurations (15 agent CLIs such as OpenCode, Claude Code, Codex; 5 hosted models: GPT-5.5, Claude-Opus-4.8, GLM-5.2, Qwen-3.7-Max, DeepSeek-V4-Pro) with a GLM-5.2 judge.
papers.code_notes: Verified via the GitHub tree API: 1,146 files, 143 Python files, including OpenART/framework/, tests/, docs/ (14 guides), target/attacker configs, a ~374 KB run_graph_rl_attacker.py (the graph attacker), three bundled 100-node tasks and a managed tool store (openart-tools/). Quickstart has install steps, Docker image builds, and a no-credential local smoke run. Only 3 high-complexity tasks are bundled, not the full 10K scenarios. I did not execute anything.
papers.feasibility_notes: All reported experiments use hosted frontier models as target, attacker and judge, and every run needs Docker (separate attacker/target containers, per-agent CLI images), which a single-GPU sandbox usually does not offer. The endpoints are OpenAI-compatible so a local vLLM model could be plugged in, but a <=8B model is very unlikely to complete 100-node, ~97-tool-call workflows, so attack-success numbers would be uninformative within 45 minutes.
papers.followup_evidence: None found. Semantic Scholar API returned citationCount 0 with an empty citations list. Web searches for "OpenART" + EMHA + "builds on / extends / follow-up / building on OpenART" returned only the paper itself, its repo, HF/alphaXiv pages, a newsletter, and a benchmark-listing issue (OpenTAI/opentai.github.io #61), none of which is a later paper.

papers.title: Dream-RSI: Recursive Self-Improvement through Evolving Worlds
papers.what_it_is: Dream-RSI improves the exploration policy of an LLM-driven discovery system (AlphaEvolve-style) by turning past discovery trees into a replay simulator and scoring candidate policies offline ('dreaming') instead of with expensive online runs. Experiments are on Lasso path algorithm discovery, math optimization (circle packing, sum-difference, autocorrelation inequalities) and KernelBench GPU kernels, all driven by Gemini-3.1 Pro / Gemini-3.7-Flash through Gemini CLI.
papers.code_notes: Placeholder. GitHub tree API shows 21 files: README.md, CITATION.cff, .gitignore, the paper PDF and logo/figure assets; no source code. The README says the code is being prepared for release, with codebase, discovered programs and reproduction scripts all pending. An unofficial third-party re-implementation exists (Harkit2004/dream-rsi-skill) but it is not the authors' code and I did not inspect it.
papers.feasibility_notes: The method depends on a strong hosted coding agent (Gemini) making hundreds to thousands of discovery calls, and no official code or logged discovery trees are released to replay. With no code and <=8B open models as the discovery agent, a 45-minute run would not produce informative results. is_nlp is borderline: it is an LLM-agent/search paper, not language processing as such.
papers.followup_evidence: No building-on work found, but it is already cited 8 times (Semantic Scholar citations endpoint): 2610.00675 LabBook, 2609.39632 Towards Better Exploration in Sequential Test-Time Scaling, 2609.39392 Experimental Experience Modeling for Autonomous Research, 2609.38812, 2610.00825, 2609.32984 ReVision3D, 2609.30001, 2609.28919. I read the arXiv HTML of the three closest (LabBook, Sequential Test-Time Scaling, Experimental Experience Modeling): each cites Dream-RSI only in related work or references, not as a baseline or extension. The other five were judged from titles only (not opened); ReVision3D (recursive self-improvement for 3D medical perception) is the one that could conceivably borrow the method. Web searches for "Dream-RSI" + builds on / extends / unlike / compared to found only news coverage and the unofficial skill repo.

papers.title: OmniEdu: Open Foundation Models for Learning and Teaching
papers.what_it_is: OmniEdu builds a ~70K-example education instruction-tuning corpus from 100+ sources (cleaned and rewritten with an open Qwen 122B model) and fully fine-tunes Qwen3.5-4B, Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.8-27B into K-12 solver/tutor models. Experiments compare these against base models and GPT-5 variants on curriculum grounding (K12-Bench, MathFish, EDUMATH), K-12 problem solving (GAOKAO-Bench, EXAMS-V, MDK12-Bench) and tutoring benchmarks (MathTutorBench, TutorBench, LongTutor), the last partly LLM-judged.
papers.code_notes: Not real code. GitHub tree API shows exactly 4 files: .gitignore, README.md, index.html, style.css (a project page). The README only has Transformers/vLLM inference snippets and links to Hugging Face weights (4B/9B/27B) and the training dataset; there is no training, data-pipeline or evaluation code. Weights and data are public on Hugging Face (not downloaded or checked by me).
papers.feasibility_notes: The released OmniEdu-4B checkpoint and its Qwen3.5-4B base fit one A100, and exact-match/accuracy benchmarks can be subsampled to run in 45 minutes; e.g. compare OmniEdu-4B vs its base on a few hundred MathFish or GAOKAO-Bench items, or a short LoRA ablation on one capability slice of the 70K corpus. Caveats: with no released eval code the paper's prompts and scoring would have to be re-created, the 9B/27B models exceed the 8B limit, and tutoring metrics that need an LLM judge are not reproducible without an API.
papers.followup_evidence: None found. Semantic Scholar citations endpoint returned an empty list (the main paper endpoint was rate-limited with HTTP 429, so citationCount was not read directly). Web searches for "OmniEdu" + builds on / extends / benchmark and for "OmniEdu-4B" / "OmniEdu-9B" / "OmniEdu-27B" returned only the paper, repo, news alerts and a community GGUF quantization (prithivMLmods/Omni-Edu-9B-GGUF), no later paper. The paper is under two weeks old.

papers.title: ModularRSI: Modular and Generalizable Recursive Harness Self-Improvement
papers.what_it_is: ModularRSI splits a coding/terminal agent harness into five modules (agent loop, tool use, observation management, context management, completion detection) and evolves each one separately from contrastive success/failure trajectories on 2,000 tasks disjoint from the evaluation benchmarks. The experiments evolve the harness with hosted DeepSeek-V4-Flash models and evaluate the frozen result on Terminal-Bench 2.0 and SWE-Bench Verified, including transfer to GLM-5.2 and MiniMax-2.5.
papers.code_notes: https://github.com/IQuestLab/ModularRSI is a real Python repo (about 73 MB, pushed 2026-09-24): src/harbor, adapters, packages/rewardkit, tests, scripts/evolve.sh and scripts/evaluate.sh, frozen evolved modules and trajectories. It needs API keys in .env and the Harbor Docker task environments. I read the file listing and README summary but did not run anything.
papers.feasibility_notes: Evolution and evaluation both run through hosted LLM APIs (the paper cites a 2M tokens-per-minute limit) and Docker sandboxes for long-horizon terminal and SWE tasks. An open model of 8B or less on one A100 for 45 minutes cannot give an informative Terminal-Bench or SWE-Bench signal, and the environment has no paid APIs.
papers.followup_evidence: None found. Semantic Scholar shows 1 citation: MemCodex (arXiv 2609.39765, 2026-09-30), which cites it in related work only (checked in the HTML). RRSI (arXiv 2609.24972) is concurrent harness self-improvement work and does not mention ModularRSI. Two web searches on "ModularRSI" with builds on / extends / follow-up / baseline returned only coverage of the paper itself.

papers.title: Random Attention: Rethinking KV Cache Eviction for Efficient Reasoning
papers.what_it_is: Random Attention is a KV-cache eviction policy for reasoning models that protects the prompt and evicts generated-trace tokens uniformly at random per attention head, with no scoring. The experiments compare it with H2O, SnapKV, R-KV, VaSE, TriAttention and StreamingLLM on Qwen3-4B/14B/32B and Phi-4-reasoning across MATH-500, AIME, HMMT, GPQA-Diamond and LiveCodeBench, plus throughput benchmarks and mechanism studies (prompt protection, planted-fact probes, fork replays).
papers.code_notes: https://github.com/SalesforceAIResearch/Random-Attention is real code (Python, Apache-2.0, pushed 2026-09-04). The file tree has kvcompress/engine (all eviction modes in cache_utils.py, modified forwards, engine tests), harness (eval_hf.py and a sharded launcher), eval (graders, paired significance tests), analysis, and synth (the synthetic-retrieval study), plus scripts/run_cell.sh, grade_cell.sh, efficiency and vLLM benchmarks, setup.sh and requirements.txt. Local Hugging Face checkpoints only, and TriAttention calibration stats for Qwen3-4B are included. Not executed by me.
papers.feasibility_notes: Everything runs on local open checkpoints; Qwen3-4B (and the optional DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B) fit on one A100 80GB, and scripts/run_cell.sh runs a single model/task/method/budget cell. Example: on a 50-100 problem MATH-500 subset with Qwen3-4B, compare random_pp with and without prompt protection, or vary the recency window or budget K, or run the planted-fact probe at different distances. Caveats: the paper used 8x H200 with a 32k-token generation cap and multiple runs, so a 45-minute budget forces subsampling and probably a shorter cap, and the setup pins torch 2.4.0, flash-attn 2.7.3 and transformers 5.0.0.
papers.followup_evidence: None found. Semantic Scholar returns citationCount 0. Two web searches (title/method with follow-up / extends / builds on, and with the arXiv id plus 'cited random eviction baseline') returned only the paper, its repo and news coverage. One related hit, "Trust the Mass: Forced Weights in KV-Cache Eviction" (arXiv 2608.25230), has an August id that predates this paper, so it is not a follow-up. The paper is only about four weeks old, so indexing may lag.

papers.title: Co-Evolution in Agentic Systems: Toward Self-Directed Evolution Beyond Human Design
papers.what_it_is: A survey of co-evolution in agentic systems that proposes a three-stage taxonomy: agent-agent, agent-environment, and meta co-evolution. It has no experiments; it organises existing literature and discusses open challenges.
papers.code_notes: https://github.com/zongqing0068/awesome-co-evolution contains only README.md and two images in assets/. It is a curated paper list, with no code.
papers.feasibility_notes: A survey has no method, benchmark or result to rerun or extend, so there is no well-defined small follow-up experiment anchored on it.
papers.followup_evidence: None found. Semantic Scholar returns citationCount 0, and a web search on the exact title returned only the paper's own pages and unrelated earlier surveys.

papers.title: Spark-to-Paper: End-to-End Research Paper Generation as a Composable Skill
papers.what_it_is: Spark-to-Paper is an end-to-end research-paper generation pipeline packaged as thirteen composable skills that run inside Claude Code (literature retrieval, experiment planning and execution, figure generation, integrity checks, self-review). Its experiments generate full manuscripts on eight topics and measure citation validity, figure editability, fabrication detection and review precision, at about 11.9M tokens, $8.1 and 3.2 hours per manuscript.
papers.code_notes: Repository has 359 files, 168 of them Python, plus SKILL.md files for each skill (skills/ts-paper-cite, ts-paper-experiment, ts-figure-svg, ts-idea2story, ts-kg-build, etc.), a .claude-plugin manifest, and showcase PDFs. It is a real, installable Claude Code plugin, but the Python is helper tooling (linting, citation checking, figure rendering); the pipeline itself only runs when driven by a Claude model. I listed the tree through the GitHub API and read the README summary; I did not run anything.
papers.feasibility_notes: The system is driven by a Claude-family model inside Claude Code, with optional paid image and vision model keys, and one run takes about 3 hours and $8, so neither the method nor its evaluation fits a 45-minute, no-paid-API budget. Only the deterministic helper scripts (for example the citation linter) could be exercised offline, and that would not be an informative test of the paper's claims.
papers.followup_evidence: None found. Semantic Scholar reports citationCount 0 for arXiv:2608.11924. Web searches for "Spark-to-Paper" with "composable skill", and with "builds on / extends / baseline", returned only the paper itself, its repo and project page, and aggregator listings; the other hits (PaperOrchestra 2604.05018, SPARK 2608.30214, PaperCompiler 2609.02272) are unrelated or earlier work.

papers.title: ScienceIDE: Turning World's Scientific Codebase into Agent Learnable Environments
papers.what_it_is: ScienceIDE converts scientific simulation codebases (PLUTO, Athena++, MITgcm, LAPS, PHANTOM and others) into containerized environments where agents repair injected defects or implement missing functionality and are graded by numerical correctness of the simulation output. Experiments compare fifteen agent models on an 85-task hard subset and train PhAI-IDE-4B/9B/72B models with LoRA SFT and GRPO-style RL on verified trajectories.
papers.code_notes: Repository has about 6,600 files (671 Python, 305 shell, Dockerfiles, task configs): environments/ with 15 published environments (agent and verifier Dockerfiles, defect injection, grading scripts), hard85/ with 30 of the 85 hard tasks, SFT/train.py with only a small sample dataset, and RL/ with agent loop, reward, runner, eval and tests. The README calls it a preview release; the full environment set, task bank and authoring pipeline are stated to live in a separate Gen-Verse/ScienceInfra repository, which I did not inspect. Tree listed through the GitHub API; nothing was run.
papers.feasibility_notes: Each task needs Docker containers that build and run real scientific simulation codes under a one-hour episode budget, demonstrations were collected with GPT-5.6-sol, and the agent comparison uses proprietary models through Codex, Claude Code and Gemini CLI. Even evaluating the released 4B model on a few tasks would not fit 45 minutes on 4 CPU cores, and container builds may not be possible in the execution sandbox at all; the released SFT data is only a small sample.
papers.followup_evidence: None found. Semantic Scholar lists 1 citation: "JEPA-Anything: Learning Predictive Models across Different Worlds" (arXiv 2609.20800, 2026-09-17), a predictive world-model paper that appears to be a passing citation; I did not open it to confirm. ScienceBuddy (arXiv 2609.17523, Gen-Verse) is a contemporaneous sibling project released a day earlier, and its repo does not say it builds on ScienceIDE. Web searches for "ScienceIDE" with PhAI-IDE, "ScienceIDE-Hard", "builds on / extends" returned only the paper, repo, a fork (ktwu01/ScienceAccelBench-fork) and news coverage.

papers.title: SpeakerMem-R1: Speaker-Centered Dual-Track Memory for Multi-Party Dialogue
papers.what_it_is: SpeakerMem-R1 is a memory system for multi-party dialogue that keeps speaker-labeled verbatim messages alongside structured person-level and group-level memories written by a Writer model, and trains a Qwen2.5-3B Writer with a SpeakerLevenshtein reward and speaker-conditioned GRPO. Experiments are question-answering accuracy on GroupMemBench, SocialMemBench, EverMemBench and LoCoMo against memory and retrieval baselines, plus a 305-question held-out comparison of SFT, RL and LLM writers.
papers.code_notes: Repository contains an installable package (code/speakermem_pkg with tests and examples), benchmark runners (run_baseline.py, run_locomo.py, examples/socialmembench.py), metric code, and writer training code (sft.py, train_process_grpo.py, training_rewards.py, training_rollout.py) with 15 training networks, teacher trajectories and 10 held-out networks, plus about 3,000 question-level result JSONL files. Not included: Writer-R1 weights and the benchmark payloads, which must be downloaded from public sources listed in DATA_SOURCES.md (Hugging Face anon4data/socialmembench, UCSB-NLP-Chang/GroupMemBench, EverMind-AI/EverMemBench-Dynamic, snap-research/locomo). README and file tree read directly; nothing was run.
papers.feasibility_notes: The paper's headline numbers use hosted models (DeepSeek-V4-Flash and GPT-5.6-luna as writer/answerer, GPT-4o-mini and Gemini-3-Flash as judges), so they cannot be reproduced exactly, but the pipeline accepts any OpenAI-compatible endpoint and a locally served writer, the verbatim track and retrieval need only a small embedding model, and token-F1 and the SpeakerLevenshtein reward need no judge. Example: on the 10 held-out SocialMemBench networks (305 questions), serve an open model of at most 8B with vLLM as answerer and compare verbatim-only versus dual-track retrieval, or vary System 1 top-k, scoring with token-F1; the caveat is that results with a small open answerer and no released Writer-R1 weights may not match the paper's setting, and a full RL writer run (30 rollout rounds, compute not reported) probably does not fit 45 minutes.
papers.followup_evidence: None found, but only partly verified: the Semantic Scholar API returned HTTP 429 on every attempt for arXiv:2609.26780, so I have no citation list for it. Web searches for "SpeakerMem-R1" / "SpeakerMem" with "multi-party dialogue memory", "builds on", "extends", "compared baseline" returned only the paper, its repo and project page, a blog post and news summaries; Memory-R1 (2508.19828) and 2605.04811 are earlier work. The paper was posted about ten days before this check.

papers.title: EvoDuet: Bilevel Co-Evolution of Web Searching and Task Solving for Scientific Discovery
papers.what_it_is: EvoDuet is a bilevel LLM-driven evolutionary search scaffold in which an outer loop evolves candidate programs/solutions and an inner loop evolves web-search queries, linked by a retrieval gate that decides whether to fetch new documents, reuse stored ones, or go without. Experiments run about 100 iterations on 31 scientific-optimization / program-evolution tasks (math, astrodynamics, quantum compilation, algorithm engineering) with GPT-5.6-Luna, Gemini-3.8-Flash and Qwen3.5-9B, reporting normalized score gains over search-free scaffolds.
papers.code_notes: https://github.com/Open-Galapagos/EvoDuet is a real Apache-2.0 Python package (about 2400 tree entries via the GitHub API): skydiscover/evoduet/ (retrieval gating, Tavily retrieval, query construction, scoring, prompts), skydiscover/evoduet_cli.py, scripts/run_evoduet.sh and baselines, benchmarks/, best_programs/, tests/evoduet/, pyproject.toml, uv.lock. README requires OPENAI_API_KEY or OPENROUTER_API_KEY plus TAVILY_API_KEY. Not executed by me.
papers.feasibility_notes: The method depends on hosted LLMs (OpenAI/OpenRouter) and the paid Tavily web-search API; the paper reports a mean cost of about $45.56 per run over 100 iterations, and its only open model (Qwen3.5-9B) is above the 8B cap. It is borderline NLP (LLM agent + retrieval applied to scientific program evolution, not language processing itself). A no-API, 45-minute follow-up would not be informative about the paper's claims.
papers.followup_evidence: None found. Semantic Scholar API returned citationCount 0 with an empty citations list. Web search for "EvoDuet" bilevel co-evolution web searching task solving returned only the paper itself, aggregator pages and daily arXiv digests. The paper was posted 2026-09-30, two days before this check.

papers.title: AURORA-LM: Autoencoding Unified Representation for Continuous-Latent Diffusion Language Modeling
papers.what_it_is: AURORA-LM is a continuous-latent diffusion language model: a query-based text autoencoder produces a high-capacity decodable latent sequence, and a block-causal diffusion transformer trained with flow matching models its distribution (with a restricted noisy-input pathway, width-calibrated noise schedule and self-trajectory consistency). Experiments are OpenWebText unconditional generation (Gen-PPL, MAUVE, entropy) and XSum summarization (ROUGE) at 130M scale, plus a 1B model on nine few-shot benchmarks, with sampler/schedule ablations.
papers.code_notes: https://github.com/fyv587/AURORA-LM contains real code (verified via GitHub tree API and raw README): src/aurora/ with models (encoder, decoder, denoiser, block-causal masks), sampling (block_sampler, solvers), train (ae_trainer, diffusion_trainer), eval (pipeline, PPL/MAUVE/ROUGE metrics), Hydra configs in conf/, data preparation scripts, train_ae/train_diffusion shell scripts, generate.py, requirements.txt, pyproject.toml. Training and inference code was released 2026-09-19 with three AURORA-LM-S checkpoints on Hugging Face (fyv587/aurora-gpt2-owt, aurora-gpt2-xsum, aurora-text-autoencoder). The 1B AURORA-LM-L checkpoint is NOT released. I did not run the code or confirm the Hugging Face weights download.
papers.feasibility_notes: Full training is out of scope (paper trained on Ascend NPUs; 1B model about 1500 EFLOPs), but the released 130M checkpoints allow inference-only follow-ups: README says one XSum pass (1000 prompts, 32 steps) takes about 11 minutes on 8x A800-80GB, so roughly 200-400 prompts per setting fit on one A100 in 45 minutes. Example: sweep sampling steps (8/16/32/64), CFG scale and sigma-window, or ODE vs SDE-DPM++ solver on a 300-prompt XSum subset and report ROUGE-L, or measure Gen-PPL vs entropy trade-off on 200 OpenWebText samples; short fine-tunes of the 130M denoiser on a small dataset are also plausible.
papers.followup_evidence: None found that builds on it. Semantic Scholar /citations endpoint (after several 429 retries) lists 4 citing papers; I opened each: (1) arXiv 2610.01016 "Scaling and Distilling Text Embeddings for Better Diffusibility" lists AURORA-LM in a results table with the number copied from the original paper (dagger mark), not re-run and not extended; (2) arXiv 2609.33698 "One Latent, Many Tokens" (JPEG-DLM) cites it in related work only; (3) arXiv 2609.04531 (PlaidQ, withdrawn) does not visibly mention it in the available abstract page, full text unavailable (HTML 404); (4) arXiv 2607.00588 is about ELF models and does not mention it in the abstract page. Web searches for "AURORA-LM" with builds on / extends / baseline returned only the paper, its repo, project page and news blurbs. The field is active, so a competing-baseline citation already exists; I count that as citation, not follow-up.

papers.title: TTPO: Test-Time Policy Optimization
papers.what_it_is: TTPO is a label-free test-time training method for LLM math reasoning: it samples many rollouts per test problem, takes the majority-vote answer as a pseudo-label, distills agreeing rollouts via on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) and penalizes disagreeing rollouts with a grouped RL loss. Experiments LoRA-fine-tune Qwen3 1.7B/4B/8B on five competition math sets (AIME 2025/2026, HMMT 2025/2026, BRUMO 2025), reporting Avg@12 accuracy against GRPO, OPSD and TTRL, with ablations on loss weighting, sample selection and thinking vs non-thinking mode.
papers.code_notes: https://github.com/ZJU-REAL/TTPO contains real code (verified via GitHub tree API): TTPO/ttpo_train.py, ttpo_trainer.py (91 KB), ttpo_voting.py, ttpo_data_collator.py, plus baselines grpo_train.py, opsd_train.py, opsd_trainer.py, ttrl_train.py; eval/evaluate_math.py with run scripts; scripts/run_ttpo_1b.sh, run_ttpo_4b.sh, run_ttpo_8b.sh; environment.yml (PyTorch 2.8, vLLM 0.11, flash-attn). 61 stars, 11 commits, last activity 2026-08-28. Example recipes assume 4 GPUs with colocated vLLM generation; I did not run it or confirm a single-GPU configuration works out of the box.
papers.feasibility_notes: All models are open Qwen3 at or below 8B with LoRA (r=64) and no APIs, but the paper setup is heavy for this budget: K=64 rollouts per problem, 100 training steps, 4x H20 GPUs, runtime per run not reported, so a follow-up must be scaled down and the 45-minute fit is tight and unverified. Example: on Qwen3-1.7B in non-thinking mode, run about 25 TTPO steps on one 30-problem AIME set with K=16-32 and compare TTPO vs TTRL vs OPSD-with-pseudo-labels, or vary the RL weight lambda / positive-negative fraction, evaluating with Avg@4 instead of Avg@12.
papers.followup_evidence: None found. Semantic Scholar API: citationCount 1, the only citing paper is arXiv 2609.33414 "TTRSD: Test-Time Reinforcement Learning with Self-Distillation for Vision-Language Models" (2026-09-27); I read its HTML and TTPO appears only in the introduction and related work alongside TTRL and TTRV, its baselines are TTRL and TTRV, so it is a related-work citation rather than an extension (though it is thematically close: test-time RL plus self-distillation, for VLMs). Web searches for "TTPO" "Test-Time Policy Optimization" with builds on / extends / follow-up and for its OPSD + Grouped RL keywords returned only the paper, a paper-notes issue, a social post, and earlier unrelated work (OptPO 2512.02882, TTSR, SERPO 2607.26873, all predating it).

papers.title: RecreationWorld: Scalable and Verifiable Environments for Hybrid Computer-Use Agents
papers.what_it_is: Introduces RecreationWorld, a five-platform (Ubuntu, macOS, Windows, Android, Web) environment in which computer-use agents explore a running reference application through its GUI and re-implement it, plus RecreationBench with 250 tasks scored by programmatic and visual assertions. It is real code, but running it needs a task bundle from Hugging Face, prepared VM/emulator environments and model plus judge endpoints. I read the file list and README only; I did not run it.
papers.feasibility_notes: Tasks need isolated GUI virtual machines or emulators, a per-rollout timeout of 20 hours, frontier-scale agent models and a Qwen3.7-Plus visual judge. Nothing meaningful fits one GPU for 45 minutes with a model of at most 8B parameters.
papers.followup_evidence: None found. papers.title: Confidence Comes from Experience: Experiential Confidence Estimation from Reasoning to Agents
papers.what_it_is: Proposes XConf, a training-free, black-box confidence estimator that keeps a bank of the model's own graded past episodes, retrieves the 50 most similar ones to read off a historical hit rate (Recall), and shows them to the model to restate its confidence (Reflect). The experiments compare AUROC and calibration error against baselines such as ten-sample self-consistency on nine benchmarks (MMLU-Pro, SuperGPQA, LiveCodeBench, MMMU-Pro, ScienceWorld, AppWorld, SWE-bench Verified and others) with four models.
papers.code_notes: https://github.com/caiqizh/xconf is a small real codebase (about 25 Python files): the xconf/ package (llm.py, embed.py, datasets.py, prompts.py, verify.py) and 17 pipeline scripts covering ingest, elicit, grade, embed, lesson, recalibrate and evaluate. llm.py includes an OpenAI-compatible client for a local vLLM server. The embedder in xconf/embed.py is hard-wired to the paid Gemini API (gemini-embedding-001), and the README says a Gemini key is needed even for local models. Agent rollout generation is not included, only an ALFWorld example driver. I read the README, file tree and parts of the source; I did not run it.
papers.feasibility_notes: The paper's own runs use Gemini 2.5/3.5 Flash, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Qwen3.5-397B and Gemini embeddings, so none of them fits the environment as-is. The method is inference-only, though, so a follow-up can serve a model of at most 8B through vLLM, replace the Gemini embedder with an open embedding model (a small code change in embed.py), and test on a subset of about 1-3k MMLU-Pro questions whether XConf still beats verbalized confidence or self-consistency for a small model, or how results change with bank size or embedder. The 45-minute budget is tight for the three generation passes (elicit, lesson, reflect with 50-episode cards), so the subset must be small; I did not time this.
papers.followup_evidence: None found. The Semantic Scholar citations endpoint returned an empty list for arXiv:2609.17708. Web searches for "XConf" "Confidence Comes from Experience" and for "2609.17708" with "builds on / extends / follow-up" returned only the paper, its repository, aggregator pages and one blog explainer (Towards AI).

papers.title: RSIGame: Autonomous Agentic Game Development with Recursive Self-improvement
papers.what_it_is: Presents RSIGame, an agentic framework that keeps improving LLM-generated games through a local explore-diagnose-repair loop and a global loop that tracks quality and keeps the best checkpoint, plus fine-tuning Qwen3.8-27B on collected traces ("experience internalization"). The experiments run 140 GameCraft-Bench tasks on two engines (Godot, Phaser) with five generators and an LLM judge.

It is real code but needs an LLM API (Claude, GPT or Qwen), Godot 4, Node 20+ with an OpenGame checkout, and a separate GameCraft-Bench install. Checkpoints and dataset were not yet released (open issue #1). I read the file list and README only; I did not run it. It counts as NLP only loosely: it is LLM code generation for games, with visual judging.
papers.feasibility_notes: Generators are GPT-5.5, Kimi-K2.6, GLM-5.3-Flash and Qwen3.8-27B; the smallest open model is 27B and also serves as the judge. A single task averages about 9M tokens, and it needs game engines and rendering, so it does not fit 45 minutes on one GPU with a model of at most 8B.

papers.title: JEPA-Anything: Learning Predictive Models across Different Worlds
papers.what_it_is: Proposes JEPA-Anything, a domain-agnostic joint-embedding predictive architecture that splits latent targets into orthogonal factors with separate predictors (orthogonal predictive factorization). Experiments train and compare predictive models across seven non-language domains (vision, single-cell biology, clinical trajectories, control, molecular dynamics, PDE fields, weather), plus a wet-lab validation.

Judged as not runnable code for the paper's experiments (partial: reusable core only).
papers.feasibility_notes: Not an NLP paper despite the cs.CL listing: the only language-model-like component is a GPT-2-small backbone over patient records. Tiny synthetic OPF-vs-JEPA experiments would fit the GPU budget, but they would not touch the paper's actual domain results, since data and domain pipelines are not released.

papers.title: SWE-bench Science: Can Coding Agents Resolve Engineering Tasks in Science?

papers.title: EVOKE: Eliciting World Knowledge in Agents for Transferable Decision-Making
papers.what_it_is: Proposes EVOKE, a post-training method for LLM agents that holds environment state and history fixed and trains the policy with a contrastive ranking loss over the same candidate actions under different goals, to elicit pretrained world knowledge. Experiments LoRA-fine-tune Qwen2.5-3B/7B and Qwen3-1.7B and evaluate on ALFWorld, WebShop and seven search-QA datasets, with ablations, data-efficiency curves and linear probes.

papers.title: LLMRouter: Unified Infrastructure for Developing, Evaluating, and Deploying LLM Routers
papers.what_it_is: Presents LLMRouter, an open-source library that puts 16+ LLM routing methods (kNN, SVM, MLP, matrix factorization, graph, multi-round, personalized) under one interface, plus xRouteBench, a 4,767-instance benchmark where every query was pre-run against 18 candidate LLMs. The main experiment trains and compares routers on quality and cost across generic text, memory, vision, time-series and personalized tracks.

I did not run anything.

Example: swap the query encoder or change the cost weight in the alpha*performance - beta*cost reward and check whether the router ranking reverses. Caveats: the original responses were collected through Together AI / NVIDIA NIM (models up to 671B), so any follow-up needing new candidate responses, or the multi-round / Router-R1 / Automix routers, is out of scope; some tracks are vision and time-series rather than text.

papers.title: SAS: Simple Attention Sparsification via End-to-End Optimization of Context Ranking
papers.what_it_is: Proposes SAS, a sparse-attention method that trains a small per-layer gate to rank context blocks end-to-end from the language-modeling loss (gate added in log form inside the attention softmax) with the LLM backbone frozen. Experiments train gates for Qwen3-4B/8B/14B on OpenR1-Math-220k and compare against SeerAttention-R and other sparse-attention baselines on reasoning (MATH500, GPQA-Diamond, AIME), LongBench and agentic benchmarks at different attention budgets.

Trained gate weights for Qwen3-4B/8B/14B are on huggingface.co/tencent/Simple-Attention-Sparsification (verified via the HF API). Evaluation depends on a forked SGLang submodule and a pixi environment; I did not run anything.

The full training recipe assumes 8 H20 GPUs, 32k-token sequences and one epoch over 220k examples, so it cannot be reproduced in 45 minutes; the eval stack (pixi, SGLang fork, custom kernels) may eat much of the time budget; Qwen3-14B exceeds the 8B limit and VitaBench needs a paid DeepSeek API key for its user simulator.

papers.title: SFT Conflicts, RL Coexists: A Theoretical and Empirical Analysis of Multi-Task Learning for LLMs
papers.what_it_is: Analyses why sequential supervised fine-tuning on several tasks makes an LLM forget earlier tasks while sequential RL (GRPO) does not, attributing it to RL producing small, sparse, near-orthogonal parameter updates, with a theoretical bound on gradient interference. Experiments fine-tune DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B (and 7B) with LoRA on math, science, code and logic tasks, measure update norms and cross-task cosine similarity, and propose Parallel-RL: train tasks separately and merge the updates.
papers.code_notes: https://github.com/GaryStack/Parallel-RL is real but thin and self-described as a 'preliminary release': 32 files, 6 Python files and 8 shell scripts (about 27 KB of code), 52 stars, last push 2026-08-04. The merging (sum/mean/TIES/SVD), LoRA/full update-geometry and score-function-statistics utilities are runnable; training and evaluation are launcher templates around external VERL and lighteval. The repo's own reproducibility map says no data, checkpoints or science reward verifier are included. I did not run anything.
papers.feasibility_notes: Marginal. The paper's GRPO setup (16 rollouts, 8192-token responses, batch sizes of 256-1024, multi-GPU) cannot be rerun in 45 minutes and no trained adapters are released, so the headline RL-vs-SFT result is not reproducible in budget. A small experiment is still possible on the 1.5B model: sample a few short rollouts per prompt for two tasks, compute advantage-weighted RL gradients and SFT gradients on LoRA parameters, and compare cross-task cosine similarity with the repo's score_function_stats; or run brief LoRA SFT on two tasks and measure update overlap. The agent would have to write the rollout and gradient-saving code and fetch the datasets itself.

papers.title: EarlyEval: Cheaper Agent Evaluation via Early Outcome Prediction
papers.what_it_is: EarlyEval trains a pair of LightGBM success/failure classifiers on features of agent-trajectory prefixes (behavioral counts, TF-IDF/SVD text, optional gold-patch overlap) to stop benchmark runs early once the outcome is predictable. Experiments are offline leave-one-agent-out predictions over about 21k pre-recorded trajectories from SWE-bench Verified, TerminalBench and Toolathlon, with MLP/BERT/LoRA-Qwen-0.5B baselines.

If the data were pre-staged, a follow-up such as swapping the TF-IDF text features for a small embedding model or testing transfer across benchmarks would fit easily. papers.title: onPanda: Efficient Annotation of On-Policy Alignment Data for LLMs and Agents via Token-Level Correction

Experiments are a small human annotator study (3 annotators x 21 image-description prompts vs POTATO and Argilla), production annotation statistics, and a token-level correction benchmark (Panda-CVL, Chinese vision-language) on which nine mostly API-hosted models are scored.
