papers.feasibility_notes: The core contribution is a human annotation tool and user study, which cannot be followed up without human annotators. The benchmark is vision-language (image description, Chinese), was evaluated with GPT-5.5/GPT-6 and other hosted or 35B models with a best F1 of about 17%, and the test set licence forbids training on it. The paper reports no fine-tuning experiments. A small open VLM could in principle be scored on Panda-CVL-test, but it would likely sit near floor and the scoring code was not found.
papers.followup_evidence: Semantic Scholar returned citationCount 0 (paper is 11 days old). Web search for 'onPanda' with 'Panda-CVL' and token-level correction returned only the paper, news summaries and the datasets; none found.

papers.title: SPADE: Self-Play in Adaptive Synthetic Executable Environments
papers.what_it_is: SPADE is a self-play RL framework in which one LLM acts both as an environment designer that writes executable Gym-style Python environments and as the agent that solves them, with the designer rewarded by hint-based regret. Experiments train Qwen3 4B, 8B and 30B-A3B with GRPO for 400 rollouts and evaluate on held-out math, science, code, Reasoning-Gym and tool-use benchmarks (BFCL v4, tau2-bench, ACEBench).
papers.code_notes: https://github.com/spade-rl/spade contains a spade/ package, training scripts (train_spade_slime.py, train_spade_tinker.py), launchers under cmd/ for 4B/8B/30B, eval_offline/, tests/, pyproject.toml, with slime and tinker-cookbook submodules; 8 commits, MIT. Hugging Face org spade-rl has Games checkpoints for 4B, 8B and 30B plus generated-environment pools and grounding corpora. Training needs WANDB credentials; tau2-bench eval needs an OpenAI/OpenRouter key for the user simulator. Not run.
papers.feasibility_notes: The method is multi-GPU RL training: the README's 30B recipe uses an 8-GPU node for 400 rollouts with SGLang + Megatron + Ray, and even the 4B recipe is far beyond 45 minutes on one A100. Only inference-side follow-ups fit, e.g. comparing the released SPADE-Qwen3-4B-Games checkpoint against base Qwen3-4B on a Reasoning-Gym subset, or measuring base-model solve rate with and without hints on the released environment pool; these are feasible but do not test the training method, and the paper has no reported compute figures to plan against.
papers.followup_evidence: Semantic Scholar lists 5 citations. Read and found related-work-only mentions: FrogNano (2609.07925), EnvHarness (2608.19880). 'Recursive self-improvement of AI research agents' (2609.26457): no SPADE mention found in HTML. Could not read full text of 'Self-Play Search Distillation' (2609.30936) or 'Multi-LLM Collaborative Alignment via Stackelberg Games' (2609.39076), so unverified. Web search also surfaced a non-paper GitHub study, ReloadLightly/spade-zero-gradient, that explicitly builds on SPADE (gradient-free designer with frozen Claude models, results marked inconclusive); it has no paper, so I did not count it, but it is a real follow-up attempt.

papers.title: Improving Test-Time Scaling with Adaptive Looped Transformers
papers.what_it_is: Proposes TaH2, an adaptive looped transformer that jointly post-trains a Qwen3 backbone (1.7B/4B/8B) with a token-level iteration decider so that extra loop iterations are spent only on tokens that benefit. Experiments are post-training runs (273K prompts, about 3.4B training tokens) followed by accuracy-versus-compute evaluation on math, code, QA and tool-use benchmarks (AIME, MATH500, HumanEval, GPQA, BFCL).
papers.code_notes: https://github.com/thu-nics/TaH holds real, runnable code, but for the predecessor paper Think-at-Hard (arXiv 2511.08577): two-stage SFT recipes for Qwen3 0.6B/1.7B, eval scripts, and TaH-plus checkpoints. The only commit after the TaH2 paper (2026-09-29, 'tah2 README') changes README.md alone, and the README news line says of TaH2 'Code will be updated shortly'. The paper's reproducibility statement likewise says code and checkpoints will be released upon publication. No TaH2 checkpoints appear under the nics-efc Hugging Face org (only TaH-plus-0.6B/1.7B and Standard baselines). So TaH2's joint training with lookahead depth supervision is not in the repo as of 2026-10-02.
papers.feasibility_notes: TaH2 itself cannot be run: no code or checkpoints, and retraining it needs about 3.4B training tokens, far beyond 45 GPU-minutes. Only experiments on the older TaH-plus-1.7B checkpoint would fit (e.g. sweeping the decider threshold on a GSM8K/MATH500 subset), which would be a follow-up to the predecessor rather than to this paper; note also the TaH backend is a slow token-by-token Python loop.
papers.followup_evidence: None found. Semantic Scholar API for arXiv:2609.35748 returns citationCount 0 with an empty citations list. Web search for "TaH2" / the paper title returned only the paper itself, aggregator pages, and earlier work (Think-at-Hard 2511.08577, LoopCoder-v2 2606.18023, 2607.20519), all predating it. The paper was posted four days before this check.

papers.title: RiskChainBench: A Benchmark for Obfuscated Platform Message Restoration and Evidence-Grounded Web Investigation
papers.what_it_is: Introduces a two-task benchmark: restoring obfuscated platform messages to recover the hidden destination (3,600 synthetic inputs), then having a vision-language web agent investigate the corresponding local website (600 human-labelled environments) and write an evidence-grounded risk report. The experiments evaluate ten hosted models on both tasks with no training.
papers.code_notes: https://github.com/mattheliu/riskchainbench-task1 (the GitHub API reports the repo as moved/renamed; the page still resolves) contains real files: HTTP runners, scoring code, schemas, offline tests, and a public input-only Hugging Face mirror (leonliuzx/riskchainbench-task1-paper-inputs). But the README itself states 'Partial reproduction only' and that it 'does not yet provide a complete public reproduction of the benchmark': gold labels, mappings, raw trajectories and the evaluation archive are withheld, and the tests are synthetic schema/scoring checks on invented fixtures. One can generate predictions but cannot score them against the paper's gold, so it is not runnable for the paper's results. I did not get the full file tree through the API (redirect), so this rests on the README and rendered repo page.
papers.feasibility_notes: All ten evaluated models are proprietary hosted APIs (GPT-5.x, Claude, Kimi, Qwen3.6 Plus, Doubao, Gemini), Task 2 needs a VLM browser agent in a BrowserGym/Playwright sandbox plus a multimodal judge, and Task 1 gold is withheld so even an open-model run on the public inputs could not be scored without requesting restricted access.
papers.followup_evidence: None found. Semantic Scholar API for arXiv:2609.16900 returns citationCount 0 with an empty citations list. Web search for "RiskChainBench" returned only the paper, its mirrors (alphaXiv, paperswithcode, pith.science) and daily-digest listings; no paper extending or re-evaluating it.

papers.title: Agent-Editing World Model: Rethinking World Modeling for LLM Agents
papers.what_it_is: Proposes an 'agent-editing' world model (AEWM) that, instead of simulating tool responses, judges each proposed reasoning-plus-action step as Critical, Exploratory or Noisy and rewrites noisy ones before real execution (EditAct), plus a rejection-sampling fine-tuning variant. Experiments train a Qwen3.5-35B-A3B AEWM (about 52B mid-training tokens plus 120K SFT examples) and evaluate Qwen3.5 4B/9B/35B agents on search, terminal and software-engineering benchmarks, along with a 3,000-decision Action Judge classification benchmark.
papers.code_notes: https://github.com/RUCAIBox/Agent-Editing-World-Model is a substantial code release (about 430 files, created 2026-09-23): the aweagent framework, EditAct scaffold and configs for search/terminal/Doc2Repo, run scripts, a test suite, and benchmarks/action_judge/evaluate.py. It is inference and evaluation only: the README says training data, trajectories, local environments and credentials are not bundled, so AEWM training cannot be reproduced. Hugging Face hosts the AEWM model (35.1B parameters) and the public, ungated RUC-AIBOX/AEWM-Action-Judge-Bench (one 331 MB JSONL with gold labels).
papers.feasibility_notes: Only the Action Judge slice fits: it is offline classification of recorded decisions with public gold labels and needs no sandbox or search credentials, so one could test how well a 4B to 8B open model judges actions zero-shot versus few-shot, or with truncated history, on a 200 to 300 example subset (examples average roughly 110 KB, so the full 3,000 will not fit in 45 minutes). The headline EditAct results are out of reach: the released AEWM is 35B (over the 8B cap), and the agent benchmarks need SerpAPI/Jina search services and Docker environments. On needs_paid_api: the agent and AEWM are self-hosted open weights, so I marked it false, but the search experiments use paid search/reader APIs and the training labels were generated with DeepSeek-V4-Pro and GLM-5.
papers.followup_evidence: None found. Semantic Scholar API for arXiv:2609.28416 returns citationCount 0 with an empty citations list. Web search for "Agent-Editing World Model" AEWM EditAct returned the paper, its repo and dataset, blog/Substack summaries, and one GitHub issue in an unrelated project proposing to try the idea (not a paper). The paper is nine days old.

papers.title: ClawGym II: Exploring Black-Box RL on Agent Harness
papers.what_it_is: ClawGym II proposes a black-box reinforcement learning framework that trains an open LLM (Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-30A3B) through unmodified agent harnesses (OpenClaw, Claude Code), by capturing model calls at a serving proxy, rebuilding them into prefix trees and applying PPO/GRPO. Its experiments are large-scale RL training runs (200-400 optimization steps with concurrent sandboxed rollouts) evaluated on ClawGym-Bench, PinchBench, JobBench and OfficeQA.
papers.code_notes: https://github.com/ClawGym/ClawGym-Agents has SFT/ and RL/ directories. RL/ contains clawgym_rl_api_server.py, clawgym_rl_rollout.py, run_qwen3_4b.sh, build_rootfs.sh, plus vendored slime and Megatron-LM and a README describing a black-box RL pipeline around the OpenClaw agent loop (Docker or chroot sandboxes, slimerl/slime Docker image, W&B key). Caveats: the top-level README cites only the first ClawGym paper, the arXiv page itself gives no repo link, and I only saw a Qwen3-4B / OpenClaw launch script, not Claude Code or mix-harness configs. I read file listings and READMEs, not the source itself.
papers.feasibility_notes: The method is RL training over long-horizon agent rollouts in many concurrent Docker/chroot sandboxes with a Megatron/slime training stack; that does not fit one GPU, 4 CPU cores and 45 minutes, and even a single evaluation pass over agent tasks is slow. The paper's rubric scoring uses GPT-5.4 as an LLM judge (hosted, paid), and I could not confirm whether the training reward also depends on it.
papers.followup_evidence: Semantic Scholar lists 2 citations: QwenGyre (arXiv 2609.33848) and WEFT (arXiv 2609.36887). QwenGyre cites it only in related work. WEFT's HTML returned 404; its abstract does not mention ClawGym, so its relation is unverified. Web search also surfaced 'What Does Multi-Harness RL Learn?' (arXiv 2609.04518), which discusses ClawGym II's mix-harness normalization as a contrasting approach in related work but does not use its code or benchmark, and Harness-RL (arXiv 2608.29641), which does not cite it. Searches: "ClawGym II" black-box RL agent harness; "ClawGym II" with builds on / extend. No clear follow-up found, but this is a crowded area and 2609.04518 is close in topic.

papers.title: PACT: Can Enterprise AI Assistants Be Trusted Under Pressure?
papers.what_it_is: PACT is a benchmark of whether LLM assistants keep following compliance rules in 12 regulated enterprise domains (48 multi-turn scenarios, 3,364 items) when users apply pressure. The experiments run 22 models three times per item and score them with an LLM extractor plus a 3-model transparency judge ensemble, aggregated into a PACTScore.
papers.code_notes: https://github.com/trace-ai-labs/pact (MIT, 19 commits, 4 stars) has a pact/ package with client.py, data.py, extract.py, metrics.py, run.py, score.py, transparency.py, plus requirements.txt and .env.example. The README documents `python -m pact.run` and `python -m pact.score`, subset flags (--limit, --reps, --groups, --modes, --domains), a --judges override, and PACT_BASE_URL for any OpenAI-compatible endpoint. The dataset is public on Hugging Face (trace-ai-labs/pact). I read the file listing and README, not the source files.
papers.feasibility_notes: As published the runs go through Baseten's paid API by default, 4 of 22 models are closed, and the extractor is GPT-OSS-120B, but the harness accepts any OpenAI-compatible endpoint and the paper itself evaluates Mistral-7B and Llama-3.1-8B, so a local vLLM server with a model of at most 8B can run a subset. Example: on a few hundred items, test whether a system-prompt variant or a specific pressure type changes violation rates for Llama-3.1-8B or a Qwen model under 8B. Main caveat: extraction and transparency judging would also have to use a model of at most 8B, so scores are not comparable to the leaderboard and judge reliability is unverified (I did not confirm in code that the extractor model can be swapped; the README says the extractor prompt is checksum-locked).
papers.followup_evidence: Semantic Scholar: citationCount 0. Web searches ("PACT" "Pressure-Applied Compliance Testing" enterprise AI assistants benchmark; "PACTScore" OR "PACT benchmark" compliance under pressure Okamoto follow-up) returned only the paper, its repo and project page, news and blog coverage, a PR adding it to an eval survey list, and a GitHub issue in another project; no later paper building on it. The paper is only about two weeks old.

papers.title: OneDayAgent: Towards a Long-Horizon Harness for Autonomous Agents
papers.what_it_is: OneDayAgent is an agent harness for multi-hour everyday tasks that decomposes a request into bounded subtasks, compresses execution memory and verifies and repairs the final deliverable. It is evaluated on the 104-task AgentIF-OneDay benchmark with five backend LLMs (GLM-5.2 primary) and a 2x2 ablation of decomposition and verification, scored by a Gemini LLM judge.
papers.code_notes: https://github.com/zjunlp/OneDayAgent (36 stars, a single commit) has src/onedayagent/ with agents/, engine/, judge/, sdk/, plus tasks/agentif_oneday/, Dockerfile, run.sh, pyproject.toml, requirements.txt and .env.example. The README describes a runnable harness needing an OpenAI-compatible LLM backend, optional VLM endpoint, Serper and Jina keys, and a separate judge endpoint. I read listings and the README, not the source files.
papers.feasibility_notes: The harness depends on paid services (Serper search, Jina page visits), hosted backends (GLM-5.2, Gemini-3.1-Pro, DeepSeek-V4-Pro for summarization) and a Gemini-3.1-Pro judge; the smallest backend tested is Qwen3.5-9B, above the 8B limit. Tasks average about 54 minutes each with a 7200-second timeout, so not even one task reliably fits in a 45-minute run.
papers.followup_evidence: Semantic Scholar: citationCount 0. Web searches ("OneDayAgent" long-horizon harness autonomous agents; "OneDayAgent" baseline OR builds on OR extends arXiv 2609) found only the paper, its Hugging Face page and an author post. Two nearby papers surfaced by the searches, HarnessDev (arXiv 2609.01437) and DAGent (arXiv 2609.39154), do not mention OneDayAgent or AgentIF-OneDay. None found.

papers.title: Puro-2B: Poor Lab's Qwen2-1.5B Trained on RTX 5090 within $5090
papers.what_it_is: Presents an open pretraining recipe (blockwise FP8 on RTX 5090s, Muon-Hyperball optimizer, curriculum model averaging, a data recipe) for training a 2B-parameter LM from scratch on up to 1.4T tokens for under $6.9K. Experiments are large pretraining runs on 24-96 GPUs plus 0.17B/0.6B optimizer and LR-schedule ablations, evaluated on 15 OpenCompass benchmarks against Qwen2-1.5B.
papers.code_notes: github.com/thu-pacman/Puro-Megatron (branch puro-2b) is a real fork of NVIDIA Megatron-LM with the MuonHyperball optimizer, power LR schedule, blockwise FP8 and packed-NPY data loading, documented in docs/puro-megatron.md. Only one recipe script is shipped (examples/puro/run_puro_2b.sh), written for multi-GPU pipeline parallelism (summarised as needing 8+ GPUs) and FP8-capable hardware; I saw no small-ablation configs or eval scripts in the repo. Ten checkpoints (Base, Phase1, Uniform, Phase2 1/2..1/16 budget, Curriculum-DecayFinal, SMA6-Inputs) and the data are on Hugging Face under thu-pacman, loadable with plain transformers AutoModelForCausalLM; the model card describes the OpenCompass eval.
papers.feasibility_notes: The headline result (1.4T-token pretraining) cannot be touched in 45 GPU-minutes, and the Megatron recipe will not run as-is on a single A100 (no native FP8, multi-GPU pipeline settings). Informative post-hoc experiments on the released 2B checkpoints do fit, e.g. comparing averaging schemes over the SMA6 input checkpoints (uniform vs EMA vs subsets) or measuring validation loss/benchmark subsets along the Phase-2 budget ladder; a tiny MuonH-vs-Muon run in a reimplementation is possible but would be weak evidence.
papers.followup_evidence: None found. Semantic Scholar reports citationCount 0. A web search for "Puro-2B" with follow-up/extends/builds-on terms returned only the paper itself, aggregator pages and blog summaries.

papers.title: Last Translation Benchmark
papers.what_it_is: Introduces a live, crowdsourced machine-translation benchmark (LTBv1: 3,456 human-authored, peer-reviewed hard examples across many language pairs, some with image/audio/video) where each example carries handcrafted pass/fail verification rules. Experiments translate the examples with commercial and open MT/LLM systems and have LLM verifiers check each rule, giving pass rates per system and a linguistic analysis of failure causes.
papers.code_notes: github.com/zouharvi/last-translation-benchmark has real code (461 commits): a Python server and TypeScript web frontend for the crowdsourcing platform, plus analysis scripts (translate/verify by extra models, autometrics cache, leaderboard scoring, paper figures). The translate/verify scripts call hosted models through OpenRouter and need platform credentials and an internal data/submissions.json, so they are not runnable offline as-is. The data is public (HF zouhar/last-translation-benchmark, 89.9 MB, and LTBv1.json) with stored translations and per-rule verdicts; a text-only LTBv1-eval subset is tagged.
papers.feasibility_notes: The paper's own pipeline depends on paid hosted models (verifiers listed in the script: Gemini 3.1 Pro, Gemini 3.5 Flash Lite, GPT-5.4 Mini, Qwen 3.7, Gemma 4 31B via OpenRouter), but the released data supports local follow-ups. Example: translate the text-only subset with an open model of at most 8B and/or use a small open model as rule verifier, then measure agreement with the stored verdicts; the agent would have to write its own inference code. I could not read the paper body (no arXiv HTML, PDF text not extractable here), so experiment details come from the abstract, README, scripts and dataset card.
papers.followup_evidence: Found LTB-AI (HF dataset OLAResearchX/LTB-AI, GitHub OLAResearch/LTB-AI, blog write-up at olaresearch.org, by Shaoxiong Ji, September 2026): 452 Chinese-English items drafted by an agentic pipeline in LTB format, with verification rules, outputs from 14 systems and LLM rule judgments, checked with the official LTB portal. This directly builds on the benchmark and method, but it is a dataset with a blog write-up, not a paper, and its author is on the LTB author list; treat as a judgment call. Semantic Scholar reports citationCount 0; web search for the title with extends/evaluated-on terms found nothing else.

papers.title: PAST-Bench: Benchmarking the Foundations of Recursive Self-Improvement in Personal Agents
papers.what_it_is: Introduces a benchmark of 26 task families (204 episodes) testing whether personal-agent frameworks improve from retained experience (memory, procedural reuse, information gathering, update), toggling persistence on and off, and proposes an improved framework, Hermes+. Experiments run four agent frameworks (Hermes, nanobot, ZeroClaw, Agent-Zero) over seven hosted models with an LLM judge, 3 runs each.
papers.code_notes: github.com/Gen-Verse/PAST-Bench contains real code (about 2,800 files, 4 commits): src/past_bench runner, graders and adapters, the task families, mock services (gmail, slack, calendar, crm, ...), vendored agent frameworks, Dockerfiles, scripts and a test suite. It requires a Docker daemon and API credentials; model profiles are all hosted models (MiniMax-M2.7, GLM-5.1, Kimi K2.6, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, GPT-5.4), with no local-model path documented.
papers.feasibility_notes: All evaluated models (GLM-5.1, Kimi K2.6, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, MiniMax-M2.7, GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet/Opus 4.6) and the LLM judge are accessed through paid APIs, and runs need Docker-orchestrated agent frameworks with multi-episode sequences. Swapping in an open model of at most 8B would likely fail the long tool-use tasks and could not complete enough multi-episode families in 45 minutes to be informative.
papers.followup_evidence: Semantic Scholar lists 3 citations. arXiv 2609.34988, "The Right Lesson at the Right Step: Deriving Control Updates for Self-Evolving Agents" (EvoCUE, 2026-09-28), evaluates its method on PAST-Bench office workflows per its abstract, i.e. builds on the benchmark. The other two (S3Gym, arXiv 2608.31100; Aspire, arXiv 2608.31111) I did not open and may be related-work citations only.

papers.title: SimpleOPD: Simple Tokenizer-Agnostic On-Policy Distillation for Long-Context Reasoning
papers.what_it_is: SimpleOPD does on-policy distillation between models with different tokenizers by aligning tokens that cover identical text spans, adding a student-reference KL loss and masking the advantage of termination tokens to stop length explosion. Its experiments distill a 30B-A3B long-context proof-reasoning teacher (SU-01) into 4B-35B students (Qwen3/3.5, Intern-S2, GLM-4.7, Gemma-4) with 100 rollout iterations at up to 32K tokens, evaluated on ProofBench, AnswerBench, AIME25 and science benchmarks.
papers.code_notes: https://github.com/hhnqqq/SimpleOPD is a real codebase (GitHub API: 439 files, 216 .py, 83 .sh; created 2026-08-11, 9 commits, 21 stars). It is a fork of the SLIME RL framework (Megatron-LM + SGLang + Ray, Docker image) with examples/on_policy_distillation/run-qwen3-8B-opd.sh, run-qwen3.5-35BA3B-opd.sh and a PAPER_ALIGNMENT.md mapping paper to code. Caveats: the curated ~4.5K-problem proof training set is not shipped (placeholders), and the teacher is consumed as an OpenAI-compatible HTTP endpoint; I could not verify that SU-01 weights are publicly downloadable. I did not run the code.
papers.feasibility_notes: Not a fit: the method needs a 30B-A3B teacher served alongside a 4B+ student with rollouts up to 32K tokens under a Megatron/SGLang/Ray stack, well beyond one A100 for 45 minutes and beyond the 8B cap for the teacher. The headline ProofBench metric is graded by a hosted judge (DeepSeek-V4-Flash), with GPT-OSS-120B as fallback judge on verifiable benchmarks; the method itself is open-weight, so the paid-API flag reflects evaluation only.
papers.followup_evidence: None found. Semantic Scholar lists 4 citations; I downloaded each arXiv HTML and grepped for the citation context: 2609.20511 (When EOS Tokens Disagree) cites it once in the intro among prior length-inflation explanations; 2609.37326 (Solving Without Stopping: OPD at Small Scale) cites it in one related-work clause about masking the stop token's advantage; 2609.18708 (Value Flattening in PPO) and 2609.14708 (Lightning Weave) cite it in related work only. None uses its code, method as a baseline, or benchmark. Web searches for "SimpleOPD" with builds on/extends/follow-up returned only the paper, repo and earlier work (SimCT 2605.07711, EasyOPD 2607.11012). The two topically close papers (2609.20511, 2609.37326) study the same length-inflation phenomenon, so the area is crowded even though nothing extends SimpleOPD directly.

papers.title: What Does Privileged Information Add to On-Policy Self-Distillation?
papers.what_it_is: The paper asks how much a privileged reference (answer or worked solution) given to the frozen teacher actually adds in on-policy self-distillation beyond reference-free distillation, using a new 5,319-problem suite (AMPLE-Math) where each problem has six reasoning views sharing one answer. Experiments are 100-step LoRA OPSD runs on Qwen3-1.7B and SmolLM3-3B with deterministic answer grading on a 384-problem test split plus AIME 2024/2025 and HMMT Feb 2025, analysed with cluster bootstrap.
papers.code_notes: https://github.com/xiuyuz/opsd-reference-study is real code (GitHub API: 48 files, 34 .py; created 2026-09-15, 2 commits, 5 stars, MIT). Contains training/train_opsd.py (55 KB) and launch_run.sh, opsd/ package (loss, prompts, grader, data), evaluation/ scripts, profiling/ scripts for teacher-profile analyses, data split builders and analysis/estimator.py. README gives run commands (CONDITION=answer_only SEED=0 GPU=0 bash training/launch_run.sh), dataset id xiuyuz/ample-math on Hugging Face, and two pinned environments (training, vLLM inference). The authors' raw evaluation records are not released. I did not run the code or confirm the HF dataset loads.
papers.feasibility_notes: Borderline but feasible: models are 1.7B and 3B with LoRA, no API or LLM judge, and the README states one 80GB GPU with direct-response training at about 30 minutes per 100 steps on an H100; however, a full thinking-enabled test evaluation costs 2-4 GPU-hours per checkpoint and thinking-mode training 6-8 hours, so a follow-up must shrink steps and evaluate on a subset. The reported effects are small (about 1.3 points), so shortened runs will be noisy; example follow-ups are a 30-50-step direct-response OPSD run with a new reference view or mixed views evaluated in direct mode on about 100 test problems, or a forward-pass-only teacher-profile comparison (profiling/score_views.py) across views.
papers.followup_evidence: None found. Semantic Scholar lists 1 citation: arXiv 2609.38995 (When Clipping Reverses Correction: Failure Dynamics of Pointwise Forward-KL OPSD, 2026-09-30). Its HTML lists the paper only in references/related work; it uses OpenThoughts, verl and Qwen3-4B, not AMPLE-Math or this repo (checked via page summary, not by my own grep). Web searches for the title and "AMPLE-Math" with builds on/extends/follow-up returned only the paper itself and earlier work (2607.05184, 2608.18271, 2602.04942). The paper is 15 days old.

papers.title: Flash-dLLM: IO-Aware KV Caching and Parallel Decoding for Fast, Memory-Efficient Diffusion LLMs
papers.what_it_is: Flash-dLLM is a training-free inference-acceleration method for masked diffusion LLMs that combines a fused Triton KV-cache kernel (QKV projection, RoPE and cache write in one pass, with selective refresh of influential decoded tokens) with a draft-and-verify parallel decoding scheme in which the model verifies its own drafts. Experiments measure accuracy and throughput for LLaDA-1.5 (and LLaDA-8B-Instruct) on GSM8K, MATH, HumanEval and MBPP on a single A100 80GB, against baselines such as Elastic-Cache.
papers.code_notes: https://github.com/VILA-Lab/Flash-dLLM is real but small (GitHub API: 24 files, 8 .py; created 2026-08-13, last push 2026-09-22, 2 commits, 18 stars, Apache-2.0). llada/ contains generate.py (22 KB), flash_cache_triton.py (21 KB), eval_llada.py (lm-eval style harness), per-benchmark scripts eval_gsm8k.sh, eval_math.sh, eval_humaneval.sh, eval_mbpp.sh and code post-processing. README gives the launch command and names GSAI-ML/LLaDA-1.5 and GSAI-ML/LLaDA-8B-Instruct. Only the LLaDA path is released; baseline implementations (e.g. Elastic-Cache) do not appear to be included. I did not run the code.
papers.feasibility_notes: Good fit: inference-only, open weights, and the authors' reference hardware is exactly one A100 80GB; at the reported ~210 tokens/s a full GSM8K pass at length 512 takes roughly an hour, so follow-ups should use subsets of 200-300 problems per configuration. Example: sweep the verify threshold and refresh budget, or test whether Flash-Verify's gains hold on LLaDA-8B-Instruct or at generation length 256, measuring accuracy and tokens/s. Risks: LLaDA is nominally 8B, right at the parameter cap (exact count not verified), and the custom Triton kernel needs a compatible Triton/CUDA setup.
papers.followup_evidence: None found. Semantic Scholar returns citationCount 0 with an empty citation list. Web searches for "Flash-dLLM", "Flash-Verify" and "Flash-Cache" with builds on/extends/baseline returned only the paper, repo, HF page and news summaries; the similarly named FlashDLM (2505.21467) is earlier, unrelated work. The paper is 10 days old, so indexes may lag.

papers.title: Negative Self-Distillation: Learning to Reason by Avoiding Flaws
papers.what_it_is: Proposes Negative Self-Distillation (NSD), a label-free fine-tuning method in which the model writes a question-specific 'negative' prompt that induces flawed reasoning, and the student is pushed away from that negative teacher using a token-level gate, a sigmoid-bounded unlikelihood loss and a KL regulariser. Experiments fine-tune Qwen3-1.7B/4B/8B on the MATH training set for 2 epochs and evaluate on seven math benchmarks (AIME 24/25/26, HMMT, AMC, OlympiadBench, MATH-500) against OPSD, Intuitor and TTRL.
papers.code_notes: https://github.com/Prongcan/NSD has real code (file tree checked via the GitHub API, 1241 entries): a modified verl framework with the NSD losses, 7 training scripts under scripts/4B_NSD, eval scripts (scripts/eval/eval_aime_pass8.py etc.), negative-condition generation pipelines under prompt/, and the data as parquet files (MATH train, pre-generated negative conditions, all eval sets). 15 commits, 13 stars. Not run by me. Scripts are only provided for Qwen3-4B and assume a multi-GPU layout (the script I read uses 6 GPUs: 4 actor/rollout + 2 teacher; README says 8x A100 80GB) plus Ray, vLLM and a WANDB_API_KEY env var (wandb online mode; would need to be disabled).
papers.feasibility_notes: Borderline. The paper's full training (2 epochs on MATH, about 68 s/step on 8 A100s, 32K-token eval outputs) does not fit one A100 for 45 minutes, and the released verl/Ray multi-GPU scripts would need re-configuring or a slim reimplementation of the loss. Scaled-down or training-free experiments do fit: e.g. with Qwen3-1.7B, use the released pre-generated negative conditions to measure which tokens the gate fires on (reasoning vs style tokens) under different gate thresholds or negative-prompt variants, or run a few dozen NSD steps on a few hundred MATH problems and evaluate on a MATH-500 subset with short outputs; such short runs may be noisy.
papers.followup_evidence: None found. Semantic Scholar citations endpoint (after several 429s) returned one citing paper: 'Learn How to Act from Your Own Interactions: On-Policy Self-Distillation for GUI Agents' (arXiv 2609.27307, 2026-09-23); I read its HTML and it cites Pei et al. only in the introduction as related work on OPSD limitations, without using, comparing to or extending NSD. Web searches for the title and for 'Negative Self-Distillation' with 'builds on / extends / follow-up / gated unlikelihood' returned only the paper itself, aggregator pages and prior work (Self-Distillation Zero 2604.12002, 2603.24472). The paper is three weeks old, so indexes may lag.

papers.title: SpectralShift: Effective Context Window Extension of Gated DeltaNet via Spectral Reparameterization
papers.what_it_is: Proposes SpectralShift, which reparameterises the alpha (decay) projections of Gated DeltaNet and scales their learning rate so that a model pretrained at 8K context can be continually pretrained to 32K-128K context. Experiments use a 1.5B-parameter Gated DeltaNet MoE model pretrained on 500B tokens of Dolma3 with Megatron-LM, evaluated on MMLU, LAMBADA, ARC-Easy, WinoGrande, PiQA, RACE, DROP, RULER and needle-in-a-haystack probes.
papers.code_notes: https://github.com/RUCAIBox/GDN-SpectralShift contains only a single git patch against a specific Megatron-LM commit (patches/), docs and diagrams; 7 commits, 1 star. The README itself states that the repository contains no runnable training example or standalone package and that verification harnesses are kept outside the release. No training or evaluation scripts, no checkpoints, no data. The patch is real method code but is not runnable on its own.
papers.feasibility_notes: The method depends on a privately pretrained 1.5B Gated DeltaNet checkpoint (500B tokens, global batch 1024, Megatron-LM) that is not released, and context extension is continual pretraining at 32K-128K tokens. Without a checkpoint or runnable harness, only a from-scratch toy GDN on synthetic retrieval tasks would fit in 45 minutes, which would be weakly informative about the paper's claims.
papers.followup_evidence: None found. Semantic Scholar returned citationCount 0 and an empty citations list. Web search for 'SpectralShift Gated DeltaNet context window extension spectral reparameterization' returned only the paper itself, aggregator pages and unrelated or earlier work (e.g. 'Optimal Decay Spectra for Linear Recurrences' 2604.07658, which predates it; 'Complex KDA' 2609.24797 appeared in results but I did not verify whether it cites SpectralShift).

papers.title: Discovery Foundation Models: Toward Open-Ended Discovery Intelligence
papers.what_it_is: A position/vision paper defining 'Discovery Foundation Models' as systems for open-ended scientific discovery with seven coupled capabilities, instantiated conceptually as the Zetema system design. Its main empirical grounding is GALILEO, a therapeutic-peptide discovery case study that couples computational reasoning with robotic and hands-on wet-lab experiments (IC50 measurements, organoids, multi-omics); there are no standard model-training or benchmark experiments.
papers.code_notes: https://github.com/Gen-Verse/DFM-Plans is a navigation hub: README files, assets, CITATION/CONTRIBUTING, and sub-folders (jepa-anything, sciencebuddy, scienceide) pointing to separate projects with their own repositories. 57 commits, 24 stars. It holds overview, milestones and links rather than runnable code for this paper; there is no code for Zetema or GALILEO. I did not open the sub-folders individually, so their exact contents are unverified.
papers.feasibility_notes: The paper is a conceptual framework whose evidence is a wet-lab drug-discovery loop with robots and biological assays, which cannot be reproduced or extended on one GPU in 45 minutes. It does not state which models or compute it used, so API dependence could not be verified (needs_paid_api=false means 'not stated', not 'confirmed absent').
papers.followup_evidence: Semantic Scholar citations endpoint lists two citing papers: 'ScienceIDE: Turning World's Scientific Codebase into Agent Learnable Environments' (arXiv 2609.19134, 2026-09-16) and 'JEPA-Anything: Learning Predictive Models across Different Worlds' (arXiv 2609.20800, 2026-09-17). Both are named in the DFM-Plans README as component projects of the DFM programme from the same group, so they are companion works building on the framework rather than independent follow-ups; I did not read either paper to confirm how they use it. Web search for 'Discovery Foundation Models Zetema builds on / extends / benchmark follow-up' found no independent follow-up.

papers.title: CogEvol: Towards Efficient and Reliable Learning Environment Generation
papers.what_it_is: CogEvol is a family of post-trained Qwen models (4B released, 27B in production) that turn a course brief into structured-JSON slides or an interactive HTML page in one pass, trained with SFT followed by GRPO using hybrid rule plus VLM-judge rewards. The experiments are production latency statistics and quality scores on private slide and HTML-500 benchmarks judged by Gemini 3.1 Pro and a 27B Qwen VLM.
papers.code_notes: https://github.com/CogEvol/CogEvol-4B (6 commits) is a model-release/deployment repo: scripts/serve.sh for llama.cpp, an OpenMAIC patch, and two small eval scripts (eval/slide_eval.py, eval/html_eval.py) that only generate outputs and check the JSON contract / extract HTML, with 3 sample cases each. The README states no training code is included; the reward system, data pipeline, 53,687 training samples and the benchmarks (slide-std, slide-short, HTML-500) are not released. Runnable for inference, but it does not implement the paper's method or evaluation.
papers.feasibility_notes: The 4B weights run locally, but the paper's quality metrics need a Gemini 3.1 Pro judge (slides) and a 27B VLM plus Playwright probes (HTML), and the benchmarks and training data are private; training used 8-16 H800 GPUs per RL stage. Only format-validity/speed checks on 3 sample cases are possible in the environment, which is not informative.
papers.followup_evidence: None found. Semantic Scholar API: citationCount 0, citations []. Web search for "CogEvol" with follow-up / builds on / extends returned only the paper itself, its repo, HF model page and aggregator pages.

papers.title: PaperGym: Rubric-Centered Evolution for Research-Plan Generation
papers.what_it_is: PaperGym converts arXiv papers into low-leakage research-plan training environments (question from goal/background, rubric from method/experiments; PaperGym-20k) and trains Qwen3 1.7B/4B/8B in two stages: rubric-conditioned self-distillation (OPSD) then GRPO with rubric-based reward. Experiments are rubric-judged scores on PaperGym-Innov/Design, ResearchQA, ResearchPlanGen-ML and RubricHub Science against SFT and larger hosted baselines, plus leakage, stability and entropy analyses.
papers.code_notes: https://github.com/ZJU-REAL/PaperGym (13 commits, MIT). Top-level README is a stub (65 bytes), but the tree has real code: data_generation/ (paper processing and problem/rubric generation), opsd/ (TRL-based SFT and self-distillation trainers, ~76KB trainer files, run scripts), grpo/ (verl launch script, reward functions, train/test parquet), and test/ (generation and scoring scripts for each benchmark, leakage detector, stability and entropy analyses, with data parquets included). Scripts contain <YOUR_MODEL_PATH>-style placeholders that must be filled in; the opsd README and several comments are in Chinese; the PaperGym test README mentions a test_mock.py that is not in the tree. Trained 1.7B/4B/8B checkpoints (CabbageWyh/PaperGym-Model) and PaperGym-Data are public and ungated on Hugging Face. I did not run any of the code.
papers.feasibility_notes: The paper's dataset construction (DeepSeek-V4-Flash, Qwen3-235B) and official evaluation judges (DeepSeek-V4-Flash, Kimi K2.6, GLM-5.1, Gemini 3.7 Flash) are hosted models, and full training used 4 A6000s, so the paper's numbers cannot be reproduced exactly. However the GRPO reward judge is a local Qwen3-4B, the scoring scripts accept any OpenAI-compatible endpoint including local vLLM, and rubrics, test sets and checkpoints are released, so small experiments fit: for example, score base Qwen3-1.7B versus released PaperGym-1.7B on a 100-200 item subset of PaperGym-Innov with a local Qwen3-4B/8B judge and test sensitivity to judge size or rubric subsets, or run a few dozen OPSD steps on the 1.7B model. Caveat: a local small judge deviates from the paper's judges, so results are indicative, not comparable.
papers.followup_evidence: None found. Semantic Scholar API lists citationCount 1, but the one entry is "Enhancing Rubric-based RL via Self-Distillation" (arXiv 2607.18082, dated 2026-07-20), which predates PaperGym and appears to be the prior self-distillation work PaperGym builds on (likely a Semantic Scholar direction artefact), not a follow-up; I did not open that paper to confirm. Web searches for "PaperGym" with builds on / extends / PaperGym-20k benchmark returned only the paper, repo, project page and aggregators.

papers.title: WearableQA: A Benchmark for Health Reasoning over Real-World Wearable Data
papers.what_it_is: WearableQA is a benchmark of 4,084 ten-option multiple-choice questions built from real wearable time series (up to about 500 days), blood biomarkers and demographics of 200 users, organised into 16 question types along data-vs-health and single-vs-cross-signal axes. The experiments evaluate 14 LLMs (6 proprietary, 8 open from Llama-3.2-3B to Llama-3.3-70B) with direct and chain-of-thought prompting, plus serialization-format, image and Python-agent ablations.
papers.code_notes: Borderline. https://github.com/facebookresearch/WearableQA (1 commit) contains the benchmark itself (WearableQA.jsonl 306 MB via Git LFS, WearableQA_raw.json 39 MB) and one dependency-free script, render_raw.py, that re-renders prompts in row/col/csv/markdown serializations. There is no evaluation harness, no model-inference code and no benchmark-construction pipeline; scoring is simple letter matching the user must write. Data is also on Hugging Face (facebook/WearableQA, ungated, CC-BY-NC-4.0). I marked this true because the released script is runnable and reproduces the exact prompts, but a strict reading (code for the paper's experiments) could say false.
papers.feasibility_notes: Evaluation is plain MCQ inference and 8 of the 14 models are open, so no API is required; an 8B-or-smaller model can be run on a subset. Constraints: prompts are very long (306 MB / 4,084 is roughly 75 KB, likely 30k+ tokens each), so only a few hundred questions fit in 45 minutes, and small models are near floor (Llama-3.2-3B 19.6%, Gemma-3-4B 19.8% versus 10% chance), which limits how informative differences will be. Example: on about 300 questions, compare Llama-3.1-8B accuracy with full history versus last-30/90-day truncation or pre-computed summary statistics, split by data-vs-health question type, using render_raw.py for serialization variants.
papers.followup_evidence: None found. Semantic Scholar API: citationCount 0, citations []. Web searches for "WearableQA" with evaluate / extends / builds on / evaluated on WearableQA returned only the paper, HF page and news/aggregator pages; WEQA (arXiv 2606.18147) is an earlier, separate work, not a follow-up.

papers.title: Massive Activations in Hybrid Linear Attention Large Language Models: Pre-Attention Spikes and Inter-Spike Plateaus
papers.what_it_is: A mechanistic study of massive activations in hybrid linear-attention LLMs, describing two patterns (pre-attention spikes before full-attention layers and inter-spike plateaus through linear-attention layers). Experiments are activation capture on about 100 inputs from each of five text domains across controlled 340M/1.3B Gated DeltaNet-style hybrids and 12 public checkpoints (1.2B-397B), plus two inference-time interventions (zeroing top coordinates; a reference-conditioned spike-to-plateau connection) scored on 11 downstream benchmarks.
papers.code_notes: Real Python package, verified from the file tree: src/massive_activations_hla (capture hooks, model loading, PAS/ISP metrics, lifecycle, plotting), three scripts (run_morphology.py, run_pas_isp_metrics.py, run_lifecycle_atlas.py), configs, tests, quickstart scripts, and 340M GDN checkpoints on Hugging Face (startlux-models/Massive-Activations-HLA). Caveat: only the analysis side is released. I found no code for the intervention experiments (coordinate zeroing, spike-to-plateau connection) or the downstream benchmark evaluation, and no pretraining code. It pins CUDA 12.6 / PyTorch 2.7.1 / flash-linear-attention 0.5.2. I did not run it.
papers.feasibility_notes: Everything is forward-pass activation analysis and inference-time intervention on open checkpoints; the 340M GDN models and the small public hybrids (about 1.2B to under 8B) fit easily on one A100 in 45 minutes, though the larger public checkpoints (27B-397B) and the controlled pretraining are out of scope. Example: zero the top-k massive-activation coordinates at full-attention inputs versus random coordinates in a released 340M GDN hybrid and measure WikiText-103 perplexity and a small retrieval task, or test a reference-free variant of the spike-to-plateau connection (the paper names this as future work). The intervention hooks would have to be written, since they are not in the repo.
papers.followup_evidence: None found. Semantic Scholar lists 1 citation: arXiv 2609.24066, 'Efficient Reasoning Exploration via State-Conditioned Latent Steering with Progress Guidance' (2026-09-21), by overlapping authors; its abstract is about steering vectors for reasoning exploration and does not build on PAS/ISP, so I count it as a passing citation. Web searches for the title and for "pre-attention spikes" / "inter-spike plateaus" returned only the paper itself, its mirrors and the repo.

papers.title: DFM Mimir v1: An Open HRM Delivering Frontier Performance at 1B Parameters Using Only Permissible Post-Training Data
papers.what_it_is: Presents DFM Mimir v1, a 1B-parameter Danish/English language model with the HRM-Text (hierarchical recurrent) architecture, trained from scratch on a mixture of 161 permissibly licensed datasets (about 70.5B tokens per epoch). The main experiment is one large training run (8 B200 GPUs, just under 3 weeks, 1.65M steps) followed by evaluation on 20 English, math/code and Danish benchmarks against HRM-Text 1B, Qwen 3.5 and Gemma 4 small models.
papers.code_notes: Real and large: a fork of sapientinc/HRM-Text, 264 commits ahead and 23 behind upstream, about 2,100 files. It contains pretrain.py (FSDP2), models/, evaluation/, conversion/, an inference engine, and Mimir/DFM-specific configs, docs and scripts (config/mimir_*.json, config/dfm_evals_*.yaml, docs/dfm*.md, a dfm-evals submodule). Weights are on Hugging Face (danish-foundation-models/DFM-Mimir). The README itself is the upstream HRM-Text README and does not document Mimir. Attention backends are listed for SM90 (H100), SM100 (B200), MPS, CPU and a dense fallback; an A100 path is not explicitly documented, and native Transformers support is described as merged but 'scheduled for the next release'.
papers.feasibility_notes: The contribution is a roughly 3-week, 8xB200 from-scratch training run and its data mixture, neither of which can be probed in 45 A100-minutes. Only inference-time evaluation of the released 1B checkpoint is in reach (for example varying the H/L recurrence cycles on a GSM8K or Danish benchmark subset), and whether the stack runs on an A100 is unverified; the README says evaluation 'typically needs one 80 GB GPU' but the documented kernels target H100/B200. This is a borderline call, made strictly.
papers.followup_evidence: No later paper found, but this is not fully verified: the Semantic Scholar citations endpoint returned HTTP 429 on every attempt for this id. Web searches ('DFM Mimir' with HRM, follow-up, extends, builds on, arXiv 2609) found only the paper, press coverage and the model cards. One successor exists as a model release, not a paper: danish-foundation-models/DFM-Mimir-v1.5 on Hugging Face, by the same team, continuing the same training lineage to epoch 10 and citing the same arXiv id.

papers.title: Gaze as Evidence for Common Grounding: A Cross-Corpus Analysis of MapTask and MUNDEX
papers.what_it_is: A cross-corpus statistical analysis of whether eye gaze signals common grounding in task dialogue, mapping HCRC MapTask and MUNDEX gaze annotations into a shared partner/task/away scheme. The experiments are non-parametric tests, GEE logistic regressions, bootstrap and chain analyses over 5,144 MapTask reference-landmark pairs and 807 MUNDEX understanding judgments; no language models are involved.
papers.code_notes: Small but real and self-contained, verified from the file tree: gaze_analysis/ (__main__.py, statistics.py, chains.py, sensitivity.py; about 50KB of Python), processed feature tables committed in data/ (MapTask CSV 2.9MB, MUNDEX CSV 0.6MB, schema, manifest), pyproject.toml and uv.lock; run with 'uv run python -m gaze_analysis'. Raw eye-tracker samples and full annotations stay with the original corpus holders. I did not run it.
papers.feasibility_notes: Compute is trivial (CPU-only statistics on included CSVs), so re-analyses fit easily, for example a different classifier or cross-corpus transfer of the gaze-feature predictor. But follow-ups are limited to the pre-extracted features, need no GPU or language model, and the paper is behavioural/multimodal dialogue analysis rather than language-model work, so it fits the study poorly.
papers.followup_evidence: None found. Semantic Scholar reports citationCount 0 with an empty citations list. A web search for the exact title returned only the paper, its Hugging Face paper and dataset pages, and the repo. The paper was posted 2026-09-16 (MINT workshop at EMNLP 2026).
